Consolidating those systems did not eliminate every inherited data problem before production.

Matt had break-glass production access and queried live payment data using SQL to triage difficult defects. He owned on-call and severity-**1** incident response, coordinating root-cause analysis across the New York team, Mumbai and Bangalore teams, and Bottomline Technologies. While incidents were live, he ran status updates and daily leadership calls. During rollout, he also ran user acceptance testing and production validation/shakeout testing, and worked with compliance teams on data verification and regulatory traceability.

He also assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, automation, and continuous delivery were part of daily work. Teams could voice feedback and implement workflow changes autonomously rather than wait for permission.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. At **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team model and emphasis on test-driven development did not initially prevent a quality failure.

In early **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months into the engagement, as the pandemic forced work fully remote, the client reported rising defects. The team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The feedback caught Matt off guard, and the credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. A bottom-up audit found that an engineer was building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt showed those gaps openly. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. They redid the code and test cases, then used boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies to bring stakeholders, developers, and product managers together around the requirements.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client and account leadership confidence returned through the open audit and visible improvement. Matt’s stated lesson was that cultural transformation requires consistent coaching, not just process change.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. In one financial services engagement, Matt’s failure to verify the team’s operating environment had consequences for both customers and a tester.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from earlier phases. His responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup, but he relied on the existing documentation rather than confirming that it was accurate.

He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement data masking or email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. Communications containing unmasked production customer data went to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. But that did not protect the tester from the consequence: the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

This was not a controlled, low-stakes experiment within a “permit to fail” environment. Matt had assumed safeguards were in place without verifying them. Afterward, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership “day-one leadership responsibilities” in his delivery approach.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the ownership behind Matt’s consulting title.

The stories don’t establish that Matt is better than someone who stayed in-house. They do document more than project delivery: at **Accenture**, he built and ran the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers over **four years**, owning full P&L accountability, budget and cost management, hiring, evaluation, promotion, compensation, and performance remediation.

The challenge wasn’t simply staffing engagements. Many new hires lacked hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies or Agile practices. As the organization grew, managers weren’t sitting beside practitioners on daily teams. Matt had to establish how people would learn, receive feedback, advance, and be held accountable without adding management layers.

He built a deliberately flat organization with **11 to 13** practice and client leads reporting directly to him. He held the closing interview and made the final hiring decision on every offer. He established peer-based feedback using evidence from recent pairing partners, product managers, and team anchors, rather than a director’s impressions. He facilitated promotion calibration, allocated compensation, and owned the decisions to end performance remediation.

For practitioners, that included pairing junior hires with experienced mentors, protected career-development conversations, and an “I do, we do, you do” learning model. Practitioners progressed from guided to independent delivery. The organization grew to **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **two years** and multiple hires promoted.

Alongside that organizational work, the centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**. The CIC reported **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**, and contributed to **\$100M+ in repeatable business** through delivery excellence and client advocacy.

What the stories don’t establish is ownership of a single internal product across its entire lifecycle. What they document is sustained ownership of an engineering organization, its economics, its people decisions, and its delivery.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes, Matt has worked in healthcare.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt worked with a **Major U.S. Health System** from May through September **2023** on AI-powered chronic disease management and responsible AI governance.

The provider’s existing application supported conditions including diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease, but care was reactive, with limited real-time patient insights. Starting with diabetes management, Matt led work to add a data lake, machine learning pipeline, LLM-driven chat, and proactive alerting to the existing application.

Rather than delivering an “art-of-the-possible” demonstration, his team used iterative product slicing to build working, extensible software. They integrated data from electronic medical records, glucometers, activity trackers, and other devices. Patients received personalized recommendations and health insights through a mobile app, and healthcare teams were trained to incorporate AI-generated insights into treatment plans. The team delivered the working MVP in **16 weeks**.

The CIO also raised concerns about HIPAA compliance and patient privacy. Matt brought together legal, compliance, IT security, data science, and clinical representatives. He operationalized **Accenture**’s Responsible AI Framework through anonymization, encryption, differential privacy, data-access policies, and continuous monitoring and auditing, rather than leaving it as principles alone.

The pilot maintained full HIPAA compliance. Clinical teams adopted AI-generated insights into treatment planning, and the executive team approved consideration of broader AI implementation.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. Identity and access management (IAM) controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying the configuration, he assumed the IAM controls and environment boundaries were already correct. He focused on delivery pressures, relied on inherited documentation, and did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not verify whether production customer data, including names and email addresses, had been masked or scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls, rather than treating the tester’s action as the entire cause. The investigation identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Afterward, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the railroad’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform when the client raised concerns about rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The discrepancy landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery, just as the pandemic forced the team into remote work.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He audited the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. They redid the code and test cases, then reinforced the practices through boot camps, coding katas, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression. He also restructured ceremonies to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers working from the same requirements.

After the experts left, Matt paired newer engineers with seasoned practitioners and rotated pairs daily. Test cases became a visible step before implementation, checked at standup rather than assumed from dashboard coverage.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Defect rates dropped, client confidence was restored, and the failure mode did not recur after the outside experts went home.

Change data capture synchronized the platforms, and reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. A **2-day** CIC Academy course ran twice monthly over **6 months**, alongside hands-on learning in Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native development.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built and ran the organization.

At **Accenture**, Matt scaled the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers to **150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design. The documented CIC starting point was a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4**. Growing client demand required hiring quickly, but many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Meanwhile, a rigid hierarchical culture initially made people slow to share ideas.

Matt built a hiring engine across bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and job requisitions. Instead of relying only on interviews, engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through messy client briefs or wireframes live. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interviewer participation capped at **2 slots per week** to protect delivery.

New hires learned through tailored enablement, senior-junior mentoring, and rotating pair partners. The progression was “I do, we do, you do,” moving practitioners from guided work to independent delivery. Teams combined product, engineering, and design, with pair programming, TDD, continuous delivery, user research, and rapid prototyping embedded in daily work. Weekly brainstorming and peer-led tech talks created space to share ideas and learn.

He kept the organization deliberately flat: **2 layers**, with **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reporting directly to him. Team anchors kept leads informed without adding middle management. Monday allocation reviews matched people to engagements and learning tracks. Because managers did not sit beside practitioners daily, evaluations drew on evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors, rather than visibility to a boss.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners** with near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**. Across CIC engagements, **10-person** balanced teams delivered output equivalent to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment engines to cross-border workflows.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional payment systems had different message formats, client configurations, entitlement structures, and compliance requirements. The bank was building ACCESS Next Generation on Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform, but its **135,000+ clients** needed capabilities beyond the platform’s out-of-box offering. Existing entitlement changes took days of manual configuration.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a **40+ person** blended **Accenture** and bank team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, managing where native platform capabilities ended and bespoke engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, payment integrity verification through Message Authentication Codes, and payment-type-specific permissions. He also built integrations for transaction monitoring, risk-based approval routing, and sanctions screening.

For connectivity, Matt designed the centralized gateway handling message transformation, protocol translation, and payment routing across **12 countries**. He led payments data migration from regional systems, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. He also owned on-call and critical-incident response through releases and migrations.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients across 180+ countries**. Its administration engine reduced entitlement management **from days to minutes**, with bulk permission changes replacing per-user configuration.

At **RBC**, Matt’s work focused on the design of cross-border payment workflows for **RBC** Express. Fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying bulk payments, while real-time FX tools were missing. He designed initiation-through-reconciliation workflows, real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and batch processing. The deliverable was a **complete implementation blueprint**, ready for development execution. Revised payment cutoff processes also reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe system, but clients faced missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox. Matt co-created the developer portal, developed SDKs across Java, .NET, and Python, and introduced use-case-driven documentation and secure, virtualized testing environments. His team used a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather end-user feedback.

Client onboarding time decreased, and API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch. Developers could explore and test integrations without waiting on the same downstream dependencies that had delayed their work.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story of Matt’s work at **Norfolk Southern**.

Matt led the Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization as a Director at **Accenture**, on the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. The railroad’s core scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually worked through waybill and rating problems. The task was to modernize without stopping the railroad, while moving a mainframe-oriented client and waterfall-oriented account leadership toward product delivery.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map business functions and dependencies. The mainframe stayed the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB were built alongside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms, and reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. Architecture work included the Boris Exercise, SNAP-E documentation, asynchronous messaging, and anti-corruption layers for legacy integration.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace. They worked from personas through high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. Delivery expanded to **3 balanced teams**, with a transition to Monterrey beginning.

The work also hit a quality crisis: defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after code and backlog stories without clear scenarios. He brought in frontend and backend TDD experts, rebuilt testable stories, and introduced coding katas and hands-on coaching. A **2-day** CIC Academy course ran twice monthly over **6 months**. Pairing helped spread scarce domain knowledge and taught client contributors Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native practices.

The MVP launched covering **95% of targeted use cases**, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation detected fallout proactively and notified trading partners rather than waiting for customer complaints. Defect rates dropped, and client contributors gained the skills to support and manage the new application after **Accenture** rolled off.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s work at **RBC**.

From June **2012** to June **2013**, Matt worked as a Senior Technology Architecture Manager on corporate banking modernization. **RBC** was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine for its Day**2Day** Corporate Banking platform while planning to replace the aging **RBC** Express portal. Existing systems had performance and scalability limitations, lacked mobile capabilities, and offered no API integration with external financial applications. Leadership needed to determine whether the proposed platform could meet business requirements before committing further investment.

Matt conducted architecture assessments across Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture. He reviewed code, interviewed stakeholders, analyzed documentation, and created architectural heat maps comparing requirements with WebSeries capabilities. Working with the enterprise architecture team, he developed logical and system models and a transparent cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for **RBC**’s long-term digital operating model. **RBC** redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives rather than investing further in that platform path.

Matt also established the PMO across **3 organizations**: **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. He maintained the program roadmap, budget, schedule, dependencies, and reporting, with designated team contacts, daily summaries, and a task-tracking matrix. He owned engagement margin and managed staffing from early specialist architecture work toward offshore and nearshore delivery as work became repeatable.

Two additional assessments addressed specific customer constraints. Transaction and chargeback history stopped at **180 days**, while audit teams needed up to **7 years** and waited days or weeks for archived records. Matt delivered requirements and solution designs for extended historical access, scheduled reporting, and scalable exports. For mobile banking, he defined API integration points, cheque deposit requirements, and cross-browser and cross-device scalability needs.

The delivered outputs included the PMO framework, architecture assessment, mobile modernization blueprint, and reporting solution design. The stories describe assessment and planning outcomes, not a completed platform rollout.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s work at **RBC**.

From **June 2012** to **June 2013**, Matt served as Senior Technology Architecture Manager on **RBC’s** Day**2Day** Corporate Banking modernization. The bank was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as its payment hub engine while planning to replace **RBC Express**. Existing systems had performance and scalability limitations, lacked mobile capabilities, and offered no API integration with external financial applications. Leadership needed to know whether the proposed platform could meet business requirements before committing further investment.

Matt conducted an architecture assessment and gap/fit analysis, drawing on prior WebSeries implementation experience. He reviewed code and documentation, interviewed stakeholders, and assessed Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture. He created architectural heat maps and worked with the bank’s enterprise architecture team on target-system models and a cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. Workshops with **RBC** leadership connected the technical findings to business goals. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for the bank’s long-term digital operating model.

Alongside that assessment, Matt established the PMO, coordinating **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. He introduced designated team contacts, shared updates, daily summaries, and a task-tracking matrix to clarify assignments and prevent duplicate work. He also owned engagement margin, staffing, forecasts, and scope-change discipline.

When the previous data conversion lead left, Matt took over the workstream from scratch. He documented source-to-target transformation rules, planned mock conversion cycles, established reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details, and coordinated business partners, IT, vendors, and onshore and offshore teams. Separately, he delivered a mobile-readiness blueprint covering APIs, cheque deposit requirements, and cross-device access.

The architecture assessment supported a pivot away from a platform path that could not deliver, allowing **RBC** to redirect technical resources before significant spend. The PMO eliminated missed program updates, and the conversion work produced an end-to-end migration plan.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt worked on at **Norfolk Southern**.

From **November 2019 to September 2023**, Matt led Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization as a Director at **Accenture**’s Cloud Innovation Center. The railroad’s core scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The work was the CIC’s first engagement, with resistance to product-oriented delivery and a pandemic-driven move to remote work.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map business functions and dependencies. Rather than replace the mainframe outright, his team kept it as the system of record while building APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. He also used the Boris Exercise and SNAP-E documentation to define APIs, data flows, dependencies, and risks.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought its revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System interface. They worked from personas through high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. The MVP launched covering **95% of targeted use cases**, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation caught fallout proactively and notified trading partners rather than waiting for customer calls.

The engagement also faced a quality crisis: defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt audited the code and tests, exposed vague backlog stories and tests written after code, and brought in TDD experts for hands-on coaching. He reinforced test-first development through daily rotating pairs, testable stories, and **1-week iterations**. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and the failure mode did not recur after the experts left.

Matt also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course, delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Client contributors paired into the new build to learn Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts. They learned to own their backlog and priorities and gained the skills to support the application after **Accenture** rolled off.

calls.raw_text:
🐾 Here’s what Matt has built, changed, and delivered.

Matt’s work centers on Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. He has built enterprise platforms, recovered troubled programs, and built the engineering organization that delivers them.

At **Accenture**, clients needed to move beyond waterfall delivery, feature factories, and siloed teams. New hires often lacked hands-on cloud-native experience. At **Norfolk Southern**, the challenge became concrete: customers were finding defects even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. Engineers were writing tests after the code, and vague backlog stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, with full P&L accountability. He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams, embedding pair programming, test-driven development, and automated delivery pipelines. Instead of presenting methodology slides, he invited clients to watch teams work.

When quality failed at **Norfolk Southern**, Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the dashboard. He audited the code and tests, rebuilt the backlog with testable stories, and brought in specialists to coach engineers through “I do, we do, you do.” The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Across the centers, practitioners progressed from guided to independent delivery, with near-zero attrition during the first **2 years**. Teams achieved **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**. At **JP Morgan Chase**, teams outpaced peer velocity within the first **2 sprints**, shipping production code in weeks rather than months.

The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ enterprise clients**, contributing to **$100M+ in repeatable business** through delivery excellence and client relationships. Clients adopted the practices internally after engagements ended.

answer_md:
🐾 Here are the core themes across Matt’s work.

Matt’s seven themes are **Execution & Delivery**, **Org & Working-Model Transformation**, **Emerging Tech**, **Professional Narrative**, **Risk & Responsible Tech**, **Strategic & Advisory**, and **Talent & Enablement**. Execution & Delivery is the primary theme, with Org & Working-Model Transformation a strong secondary theme.

At **Accenture**, clients were asking to move from waterfall to iterative development, from feature factories to customer-centric product development, and from siloed teams to balanced teams. New hires also needed hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies and modern engineering practices. At **RBC**, leadership needed to determine whether a proposed payment platform could meet business requirements before committing further investment. At **JP Morgan Chase**, application teams needed migration plans for new identity and access management requirements following a data breach.

For **Execution & Delivery** and **Org & Working-Model Transformation**, Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers, introduced pair programming, test-driven development, and CI/CD, and brought product, engineering, and design together in balanced teams. The centers grew from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, achieving **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**. Teams of **10** delivered equivalent output to traditional teams of **20**.

**Emerging Tech** includes cloud-native systems and the engineering practices used to take them from prototype to production. **Talent & Enablement** includes tailored training, competency frameworks, and the “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression. Practitioners progressed from guided to independent delivery.

For **Strategic & Advisory**, Matt assessed **RBC’s** proposed WebSeries platform through code reviews, gap/fit analysis, and architectural heat maps. The assessment found that the platform could not deliver what the bank needed, and **RBC** redirected resources. For **Risk & Responsible Tech**, he delivered a roadmap and migration plan covering **341 applications** at **JP Morgan Chase** within a **3-month engagement**.

**Professional Narrative** covers Matt’s career progression from engineer to Director and his stated next step: building products, platforms, and teams that last beyond the engagement.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what connects Matt’s work across clients and teams.

Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement recur across his work. The starting problems were often concrete: slow iterations, late defect discovery, siloed teams, and modernization programs carrying old working habits into new technology. At **Norfolk Southern**, resistance included: “I’m not paying for two people to do the work of one.” At **Capital One**, slow, misaligned product iterations extended time-to-market and disconnected solutions from user needs.

Matt repeatedly brought product, design, and engineering into balanced teams rather than organizing delivery around handoffs. At **Capital One**, he built a team of **8**, working from a client-prioritized, testable backlog. Pair programming, TDD, BDD, and red-green-refactor supported feature delivery **3 to 4x** faster than other **Accenture** teams on the same engagement, with **zero production defects**.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what connects Matt’s work across delivery, modernization, and team enablement.

Execution & Delivery and Org & Working-Model Transformation recur together. At **Capital One**, slow, misaligned product iterations extended time-to-market and disconnected solutions from user needs. At **Norfolk Southern**, business rules lived in a decades-old mainframe, orders fell out unnoticed until customers called, and the modernization faced resistance from a client organization shaped around mainframe thinking and account leadership accustomed to waterfall. At **AT&T**, infrastructure bottlenecks and integration challenges across **10+ teams** delayed a critical CRM replacement. Across these engagements, the difficulties included both the systems and how teams worked around them.

Matt changed delivery practices alongside the technology. At **Capital One**, he brought product, design, and engineering into a balanced team of **8**, working from a client-prioritized, testable backlog. The team used pair programming, TDD/BDD, and thin-slice MVPs rather than waiting for large releases. At **Norfolk Southern**, he kept the mainframe as the system of record while APIs, microservices, and a new database rose beside it. When the client grew restless for tangible progress, he brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the application through weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

Talent & Enablement also recurs in the work. At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt paired domain experts with team members through an “I do, we do, you do” progression, rotating scarce legacy knowledge through the team. When defects rose despite near-complete test coverage, he audited the code and tests, rebuilt vague backlog stories, and brought in TDD experts for hands-on coaching. At **AT&T**, he transferred post-implementation stabilization to the offshore team.

The outcomes stayed specific to each engagement: **Capital One** delivered features **3-4x faster** than other **Accenture** teams on the same engagement, with **zero production defects**. **Norfolk Southern’s** MVP covered **95%** of targeted use cases. At **AT&T**, an infrastructure delay fell from **4 weeks** to **3 days**, and post-implementation tickets declined from approximately **4,000** to approximately **200**.
